title: A stroll around the sphere
subtitle: Quantum gates are turns on a globe. Take the arrow wherever the challenge asks.

steps.title: A globe for one qubit
body: Every state of a qubit can be drawn as an arrow inside a sphere: the Bloch sphere. The north pole is |0⟩, the south pole is |1⟩.
Latitude gives the odds: the closer to the south pole, the more likely you are to measure 1. On the equator, it's half and half.
Longitude is the phase: invisible to a direct measurement, but decisive when states interfere. And quantum gates? They're turns of the arrow.
steps.aside: In the challenges, the sphere next to the circuit shows the arrow in real time. The target shows up as a dashed arrow.

steps.title: Upside down
steps.goal: Take the arrow from the north pole (|0⟩) to the south pole (|1⟩).
hints: X is a 180° turn around the X axis, which goes through the sphere from front to back.
steps.success: X turns half a revolution: north becomes south. It's the quantum NOT.

steps.title: Off to the equator
steps.goal: Leave the arrow on the equator, pointing at you: the state |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2.
hints: H swaps the north pole for the point on the equator that faces you.
steps.success: The Hadamard is a 180° turn around a diagonal axis, between X and Z. It swaps “poles” for “equator”.

steps.title: The other side of the equator
steps.goal: Reach |−⟩ = (|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2: also on the equator, but pointing backwards.
hints: The probability bars for |+⟩ and |−⟩ are identical. What changes is the color (the phase) of the 1 bar.
Z turns half a revolution around the vertical axis — swapping “front” for “back” on the equator.
steps.success: Notice: the probabilities are the same as |+⟩, but the 1 bar changed color. The minus sign is real — it only shows up when there's interference.

steps.question: What does the Z gate do to a qubit in |0⟩?

options.why: That's X. Z turns around the vertical axis — and a point on the pole doesn't move when the globe spins around it.
Right. Z only flips the sign of |1⟩. Since |0⟩ has no |1⟩ part, it stays the same.
Creating superposition from a pole is H's job. Z only touches the phase.

steps.title: Look to the side
steps.goal: Reach |+i⟩ = (|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2: on the equator, pointing right.
hints: First go to the equator. Then turn a quarter revolution around the vertical axis.
S is “half a Z”: it turns 90° instead of 180°.
steps.success: S rotated the phase by 90°. In numbers, the amplitude of 1 gained an i — and the bar's color rotated along with it.

steps.title: Three quarters of a turn
steps.goal: Reach |−i⟩ = (|0⟩ − i|1⟩)/√2, pointing left. No gate that turns backwards!
hints: Turning −90° is the same as turning +270°.
steps.success: Phases add up like angles: 90° + 180° = 270°, which is the same as −90°.

steps.title: Who was Bloch?
steps.text: Felix Bloch shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics for nuclear magnetic resonance: measuring how the spins of atomic nuclei turn in a magnetic field. Decades later, that idea became the MRI scan in hospitals. The sphere named after him describes exactly those turns.

takeaways: A qubit is an arrow on the Bloch sphere: latitude gives the odds, longitude is the phase.
X, Z and H are 180° turns around different axes; S and T are smaller turns around the vertical axis.
States with the same probabilities can be different: phase matters.
